title: Concept Acupuncturist: An Efficient and Precise Concept Erasure Method for Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders

paper.title: Concept Acupuncturist: An Efficient and Precise Concept Erasure Method for Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion-based image generation models produce high-quality images but may generate harmful or policy-violating content, motivating machine unlearning (MU) to selectively remove target concepts while preserving general capabilities.
However, existing MU approaches often struggle with the distributed and entangled nature of concept representations, leading to inefficient optimization and imprecise edits when applied through large-scale fine-tuning over full diffusion trajectories.
To bridge this gap, we propose Concept Acupuncturist ( ConceptACP ), a novel MU framework that integrates interpretability-guided analysis with inference-free fine-tuning for efficient and precise concept removal.
By establishing mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks in the U-Net denoiser and localizing the most concept-relevant block for targeted optimization, ConceptACP avoids full diffusion trajectory optimization, thereby improving fine-tuning efficiency.
To mitigate concept entanglement, we propose a feature-level correction mechanism based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where SAE-derived sparse, semantically meaningful feature activations are manipulated to construct targeted correction signals, which are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding block and used as supervision for precise concept removal.
Consequently, ConceptACP eliminates the need for external inference-time modules while achieving efficient and fine-grained unlearning.
Instantiated on SDXL-Turbo, ConceptACP improves the forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points in the standard one-step generation setting on average over the best-performing baseline, while preserving image quality and prompt fidelity, and generalizes effectively across other Stable Diffusion backbones.
Our code is available at https://github.com/Eran-Xia/ConceptACP . Warning : This paper includes images that may contain non-explicit nudity and may be sensitive to some readers.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] have demonstrated strong capabilities in image synthesis [ 6 , 2 ] and editing [ 7 , 8 ] . Training these models on large-scale web datasets improves performance, but also exposes them to diverse and weakly curated content. Consequently, such models may produce harmful or policy-violating content, e.g., Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) imagery [ 9 , 10 ] or infringing outputs that replicate protected identities or artistic styles without authorization [ 11 ] . These concerns motivate the development of various strategies for mitigating unsafe content, including dataset curation, post-processing and direct model modification. However, retraining on filtered datasets is often computationally expensive [ 12 , 13 ] , and post-processing remains vulnerable to prompt manipulation [ 14 , 15 ] . Approaches for direct model modification, particularly machine unlearning (MU), offer a more direct and controllable way to remove specific concepts without full retraining [ 16 , 17 ] . Existing MU methods can be broadly divided into three categories: inference-time intervention, model editing and fine-tuning-based unlearning. Inference-time approaches [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] typically suppress undesirable concepts by attaching external, removable modules during inference, which modify model outputs without altering model parameters and thus leave concept-related representations encoded within the model. Such interventions may introduce artifacts and degrade generation quality [ 25 ] , while their inference overhead becomes non-negligible under large-scale deployment. Model editing methods [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] directly modify model parameters through closed-form or localized updates to remove target concepts. However, the highly distributed and entangled representations in diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 ] make precise parameter localization difficult. More fundamentally, existing methods focus on finding low-interference update directions rather than identifying the parameters or internal features that encode the target concept [ 28 ] . Fine-tuning-based MU methods, in contrast, directly modify model parameters without additional inference overhead, making them widely adopted for safer image generation. However, they still face two fundamental challenges: (i) limited edit precision, since global or layer-wise updates often interfere with unrelated concepts due to the polysemantic nature of neurons [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , making it difficult to precisely remove a target concept without affecting others; and (ii) high computational cost, as they often update a large portion of model parameters (e.g., all cross-attention layers or global weights [ 9 , 32 ] ) and require executing the denoising process up to an intermediate timestep to obtain supervision [ 9 ] due to the iterative nature of diffusion models, thereby incurring full-trajectory cost even for local updates and leading to substantial training overhead, especially when scaling to multiple concepts or iterative updates. To overcome these limitations, we propose Concept Acupuncturist ( ConceptACP ), a structured fine-tuning framework that enables inference-free and localized updates for parameter optimization. Inspired by recent interpretability studies showing that concept-related information can be decomposed into structured and semantically meaningful components [ 33 ] , we introduce Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), an interpretable tool that decomposes neuron activations into sparse feature representations within the U-Net denoiser, to enable fine-grained concept removal. We further reformulate diffusion fine-tuning as a localized block-level learning problem, avoiding full denoising trajectories during optimization. Nevertheless, realizing this design presents two technical challenges: C1: difficulty in internalizing feature-level interventions into model parameters. Existing SAE-based methods typically treat SAEs as inference-time intervention modules [ 22 , 23 ] . A natural question is therefore whether the benefits of such feature-level editing can be directly embedded into model parameters. However, SAEs operate on the residual updates of corresponding blocks and require explicit feature manipulation to achieve forgetting, making their direct translation into parameter updates non-trivial. C2: difficulty in identifying the target block and constructing reliable supervision signals. Concept representations in diffusion models are distributed across multiple cross-attention blocks and evolve over the denoising trajectory, making it challenging to identify an appropriate block and derive consistent supervision for localized fine-tuning. To address C1 , we move beyond treating SAEs as external modules but as a mechanism for constructing supervision signals. Given prompts containing the target concept, we identify concept-relevant features and suppress them according to their relevance scores via a feature selection procedure. The modified features are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding cross-attention block. This process yields target outputs that are equivalent to performing feature-level editing, but expressed in the model’s native representation space. By pairing these corrected outputs with the original inputs, we construct a supervision dataset that enables internalization of feature-level interventions into model parameters. To address C2 , we reformulate diffusion fine-tuning as a localized block-level learning problem. Specifically, we establish mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks using a pool of pretrained SAEs, building upon prior analysis [ 33 ] . Based on the mappings, we identify one block most strongly associated with the target concept together with its relevant features and then construct a block-level input–output supervision dataset from a small set of text prompts at selected timesteps. The target outputs are obtained via the feature-level correction process described above. Importantly, we collect the block’s activations across timesteps in a single forward pass, avoiding repeated denoising during fine-tuning while retaining further flexible feature manipulation through the cached activations. We implement ConceptACP on SDXL-Turbo and evaluate it on the EvalIGMU [ 34 ] benchmark across four representative concepts. Experiments show that ConceptACP achieves strong balance between forgetting effectiveness and preservation of unrelated concepts, improving forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points on average under the standard one-step setting over the best-performing baseline. We further observe consistent gains on SDXL and SD v1.4, demonstrating transferability across backbones. In terms of efficiency, our block-level, inference-free fine-tuning reduces computational cost by 46.4% compared to full diffusion-based method without this design. In addition, we introduce two metrics, Feature Overlap Score and Feature Activation Correlation Score , to characterize internal feature dynamics before and after unlearning. Results show that our method induces feature-level changes consistent with the intended concept suppression and non-target preservation, providing internal evidence for its precise unlearning. Additional results demonstrate preserved image quality and robustness against adversarial prompts. Our main contributions are outlined below: • We propose ConceptACP , a novel unlearning framework that integrates interpretability-guided feature analysis into parameter-level fine-tuning for diffusion models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to use SAE-derived feature corrections as supervision for localized and internalized fine-tuning in diffusion model unlearning. • We introduce a structured fine-tuning paradigm that jointly improves edit precision and efficiency. For precision, we use SAE-derived feature corrections as fine-grained supervision, while for efficiency, we construct block-level input–output supervision to enable inference-free fine-tuning of a single cross-attention block. • Extensive experiments show that ConceptACP effectively removes target concepts while preserving model utility and substantially reducing fine-tuning computational cost.

sections.heading: II-A Text-to-Image Models
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] synthesize realistic images by gradually denoising random noise through a learned reverse diffusion process. These models typically consist of three key components: a text encoder that converts input prompts into semantic embeddings, a U - Net denoiser that conditions on the text embedding and iteratively refines a latent representation, and a decoder that maps the latent representation back to the image space. Among these components, the U - Net serves as the core of the denoising process, comprising downsampling and upsampling pathways connected through residual blocks, often interleaved with attention or transformer modules. Traditional Stable Diffusion models, such as the 1.x and 2.x versions, typically require tens of denoising steps (e.g., 50) to generate high-quality images. To improve image fidelity and prompt adherence, Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [ 5 ] was introduced. SDXL-Turbo [ 35 ] , on the other hand, is a distilled variant of SDXL, trained with techniques such as adversarial and progressive distillation to accelerate generation. It typically requires only 1–4 steps to generate an image while maintaining competitive visual quality. Architecturally, the U - Net in SDXL-Turbo comprises a downsampling path, a bottleneck section and an upsampling path with transformer blocks to capture global context. With growing demand for real-time and interactive text-to-image generation, SDXL-Turbo has gained significant attention for its fast inference.

sections.heading: II-B Machine Unlearning
sections.text: MU aims to remove the influence of specific subsets of data or learned knowledge from a trained model [ 36 , 37 ] . Typically, existing methods for T2I models either erase individual samples or suppress undesired concepts. The latter, which has received substantial attention in recent studies, aims to significantly suppress the T2I model’s ability to generate particular undesired concepts while preserving its performance on unrelated content. The unlearning targets explored in prior research include: (1) semantics (e.g., nudity, violence, and gore), (2) stylistic attributes (e.g., Van Gogh), and (3) objects (e.g., church and parachute). Existing MU approaches can be broadly categorized into three strategies: Model Fine-tuning. Fine-tuning-based methods achieve unlearning by updating model parameters to erase target concepts. For example, ESD [ 9 ] shifts predictions from concept-conditioned to unconditional outputs, AC [ 38 ] align distributions for concept removal, SA [ 39 ] replaces forgotten concepts with alternative distributions, attention redirection [ 11 ] fine-tunes cross-attention layers, MACE [ 40 ] combines attention editing with LoRA for multi-concept erasure, and TRACE [ 32 ] constrains edits to later denoising stages. Model Editing. Model editing-based approaches aim to remove concepts without additional training by directly modifying model weights. RECE [ 26 ] iteratively eliminates residual embeddings, and ConceptPrune [ 27 ] prunes FFN neurons correlated with the target concept. SPEED [ 28 ] further improves prior preservation by introducing null-space constrained parameter editing, where model updates are restricted to directions that minimize interference with non-target concepts. Inference-time Intervention. Inference intervention-based methods manipulate prompts or feature activations during inference. SLD [ 18 ] appends concept descriptors to prompts, SAFREE [ 19 ] projects toxic token embeddings orthogonally to harmful concepts, TraSCE [ 20 ] provides trajectory-level guidance, and SafeRedir [ 21 ] redirects the prompt embeddings of unsafe concepts. Based on Sparse Autoencoders, SAEUron [ 22 ] trains them on U - Net feature activations, ConceptSteerers [ 23 ] applies SAEs to the text encoder, and SAEmnesia [ 24 ] uses supervised SAE training for clearer concept-neuron mapping.

sections.heading: II-D Threat Model
sections.text: With the rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence, diffusion-based image generation models have been widely deployed in online platforms and local applications. However, this flexibility also raises safety and copyright concerns, as users may intentionally generate inappropriate content (e.g., nudity, violence) or unintentionally produce images that mimic copyrighted artistic styles (e.g., Van Gogh). We consider two realistic deployment scenarios for T2I diffusion models in practical deployment settings. S1: Online Deployment with Controlled Access. In this setting, the service provider deploys the diffusion model online and exposes its interface for user interaction under controlled conditions. The adversaries seek to induce the model to generate unsafe or policy-violating images. Their access to the model is strictly black-box: they can only interact with the system through text prompts and observe the generated outputs. As a result, adversaries may attempt prompt-based attacks, such as carefully crafted or obfuscated prompts, to bypass safety filters in online deployments. S2: Public Release of Model Checkpoints. We assume that the model providers who host or distribute text-to-image diffusion models are trusted. Their goal is to maintain a balance between safety and utility, preventing the generation of harmful or undesired content while preserving the model’s ability to produce benign and creative outputs. In practice, such providers may share model checkpoints with the research community. Adversaries can download the released model weights and deploy the model locally with full control. They can attempt low-cost strategies to bypass safety mechanisms, e.g., by removing external modules or directly querying the base model without the added controls. Under this setting, the model provider does not bear responsibility for any consequences resulting from downstream modification to the model weights.

sections.heading: III Empirical Study
sections.text: MU methods in diffusion models have evolved rapidly in recent years. However, many design choices, including localization strategy, editing paradigm, optimization scope and evaluation protocol, remain largely empirical. In this section, we systematically investigate these design choices through a series of empirical studies. Our findings not only reveal the limitations of existing approaches but also motivate the design principles adopted in ConceptACP .

sections.heading: III-A The Limitations of Neuron-level Localization
sections.text: Unlearning methods must first determine where to edit, as precise localization enables effective concept removal with minimal interference to unrelated concepts. Existing approaches perform localization at different levels of the network. For example, ESD [ 9 ] modifies model parameters globally, UCE [ 42 ] edits concept representations through cross-attention layers, and ConceptPrune [ 27 ] identifies and suppresses concept-related neurons in the FFN modules of the U-Net. However, these approaches still rely on neuron-level or architecture-level localization, which faces fundamental challenges due to the polysemantic nature of neurons [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , where a single neuron may encode information about multiple concepts, hindering selective concept removal. As shown in Table III , although existing methods achieve considerable forgetting success rates, they often degrade image quality, suggesting that coarse localization can affect representations beyond the target concept. While recent methods such as SPEED [ 28 ] improve the preservation of unrelated concepts by constraining parameter updates to less interfering subspaces, they mainly focus on how to edit after selecting the editing space. However, achieving precise unlearning also requires addressing where to edit , i.e., accurately identifying the internal representations associated with the target concept. SAEs provide a potential solution by decomposing polysemantic neurons into more sparse and interpretable features, motivating feature-level localization for more precise concept unlearning. In Figure 1 , we visualize the six most highly activated SAE features across four representative cross-attention blocks for the same input. Notably, visual features associated with the naked concept show strong activation in the down.2.1 cross-attention block. This observation indicates that concepts are localized to specific internal representations rather than uniformly distributed across the network. Fig. 1: Visualization of the top-6 activated SAE features across different cross-attention blocks. The black rectangle visually masks the region containing nudity. Observation 1: Neuron-level localization is insufficient for precise concept removal due to neuron polysemanticity, often affecting unrelated representations and degrading generation quality.

sections.heading: III-B The Fragility of Inference-time Steering
sections.text: Instead of modifying model parameters, inference-time unlearning methods perform concept suppression during inference by introducing external modules or modifying the generation pipeline. However, such approaches remain fragile due to their bypassability in open-source settings and the additional computation incurred for each generation. As shown in Table I , we evaluate three representative methods (TraSCE [ 20 ] , SAFREE [ 19 ] and SAEUron [ 22 ] ) on SDXL-Turbo and observe that they introduce 14.4%–125.8% additional inference latency, which translates into continuous computational expenses during deployment despite avoiding one-time editing costs. In contrast, parameter editing incurs a one-time cost with zero inference overhead, whereas inference-time steering incurs continuous overhead that accumulates with the number of requests. Using a representative GPU serving cost of $4/hour based on on-demand NVIDIA A100 pricing and the original SDXL-Turbo latency of 0.6848 seconds (Table IX ), the measured overhead translates to approximately $110–$960 additional cost per million generation requests, which is non-negligible at scale. Moreover, SAEUron leverages SAEs for targeted inference-time suppression but directly manipulates intermediate representations, potentially disturbing the original feature distribution and introducing visual artifacts [ 25 ] . Together with the inference overhead discussed above, these limitations make direct parameter editing a more robust alternative, as it permanently modifies the model without additional inference cost. sections.heading: III-C The Inefficiency of Large-scale Fine-tuning
sections.text: Existing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods [ 9 , 40 , 32 ] suffer from substantial computational overhead due to both large-scale parameter updates and the iterative nature of diffusion models. These methods typically modify a large portion of model parameters (e.g., multiple cross-attention layers or global weights), while obtaining supervision at a specific denoising timestep requires executing all preceding steps. Consequently, updating even a local module remains coupled with the full denoising trajectory, leading to inefficient optimization. As shown in Table VIII , fine-tuning a single cross-attention block without executing the complete denoising trajectory reduces the per-iteration training time to 53.6% of the original approach. This demonstrates that a significant portion of the optimization cost comes from the dependency on the full diffusion trajectory rather than the actual parameters being updated. This highlights the substantial computational overhead of large-scale fine-tuning, which is not necessarily accompanied by improved concept forgetting. Observation 3: Existing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods incur substantial optimization costs due to large-scale parameter updates and full-trajectory dependency, while local updates may achieve comparable forgetting with substantially lower cost.

sections.heading: III-D The Limitations of Output-based Evaluation
sections.text: Fig. 2: Discrepancy between classifier-based evaluation and human perception after concept unlearning. Existing diffusion unlearning methods are typically evaluated through generated outputs, where classifiers are used to determine whether the target concept remains present after unlearning. However, classifier-based evaluation may not accurately reflect human perception, resulting in discrepancies between automated assessment and actual visual understanding. As illustrated in Figure 2 , generated images that receive similar classifier predictions may exhibit different levels of concept presence from a human perspective. Therefore, output-level metrics alone provide incomplete evidence of genuine concept forgetting. Analyzing internal representations associated with visual concepts can provide complementary insights into the forgetting process, yet remains largely unexplored so far in existing works. Observation 4: Output-level evaluation provides incomplete evidence of concept forgetting as classifier predictions may not align with human perception, motivating complementary analysis of internal representations.

sections.heading: III-E The Generalization Gap Across Diffusion Architectures
sections.text: Most existing MU methods were developed for Stable Diffusion v1.4/1.5. However, modern diffusion models such as SDXL-Turbo introduce substantial differences in model architecture and inference, including deeper U-Net structures and significantly fewer sampling steps. When directly applied to SDXL-Turbo, existing methods exhibit notable performance degradation (e.g., ESD), which we hypothesize is partly due to its fast-sampling regime (1–4 vs. tens of steps in standard SD). Quantitative results and visualizations (see § VI-B ) further support these limitations under fast-sampling conditions. Observation 5: Existing unlearning methods, particularly timestep-wise interventions, show limited cross-architecture generalization, as SD1.x-based approaches degrade significantly on modern fast-sampling models. Overall, these observations highlight the need for unlearning approaches that are both precise and effective across different diffusion paradigms, including traditional multi-step diffusion models as well as modern large-scale, fast-sampling ones, as addressed by the method proposed in this work. sections.heading: IV-A Overview
sections.text: Based on the empirical analysis in § III , we identify the need for a more precise and efficient fine-tuning approach. Our key idea is to leverage SAEs for feature-level localization and intervention, while internalizing their corrections into model parameters through localized fine-tuning. Unlike prior methods that attach SAEs to the final model during inference [ 22 , 23 , 43 ] , we instead use them to construct supervision signals for parameter optimization. This design introduces no additional inference overhead while embedding the unlearning effect directly into model parameters, thereby addressing S1 and supporting S2 , while requiring attackers to perform weight-level manipulation rather than merely bypass inference-time interventions. Meanwhile, we localize the update to a single cross-attention block most relevant to the target concept, thus avoiding end-to-end optimization along the full diffusion trajectory and reducing the computational cost of fine-tuning. An overview of our approach is shown in Figure 3 . We begin with feature localization to identify the block most strongly associated with the target concept, along with its corresponding features. We establish mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks, and apply the feature localization algorithm introduced in § IV-B to automatically identify both the target block and the corresponding features to be modified. This joint localization substantially narrows the fine-tuning scope, enabling faster and more targeted updates. Subsequently, we construct fine-tuning datasets by modifying the localized features controlled by a scaling factor a a (defined in § IV-C ) and projecting them back to the output space of the corresponding cross-attention block. These corrected representations serve as supervision signals for subsequent parameter optimization. Crucially, instead of performing end-to-end diffusion inference during training, we only need a single forward pass to record input–output pairs of the identified cross-attention block along the denoising trajectory, enabling inference-free fine-tuning. Finally, we perform block fine-tuning using a joint objective (Eq. ( 11 ) in § IV-D ) that balances target concept suppression and preservation of generation quality. The resulting parameter updates internalize the SAE-based feature corrections into the model, enabling precise concept erasure without additional inference-time components. The updated cross-attention block is then used in place of the original block during generation. Overall, this framework enables precise and interpretable unlearning across different concept categories.

Through extensive experiments, we address the following research questions (RQs): • RQ1: How effective is ConceptACP in unlearning compared with other methods? sections.heading: VI-A Setup
sections.text: Unlearning Tasks. Following prior works [ 45 , 46 , 34 , 9 , 42 ] , we consider three representative unlearning scenarios: global-abstract-style, local-abstract-style and local-concrete-objects, followed by four specific tasks, i.e., Nudity , VanGogh , Church and Parachute . These four concepts are commonly adopted as representative unlearning targets, with Church and Parachute in particular being widely used due to their known difficulty to forget effectively. Other unlearning tasks that can be classified into the above three categories are treated as the same type and handled with the same pipeline. Models. We conduct our main experiments on SDXL-Turbo, which supports high-quality image generation with 1–4 inference steps. We evaluate both 1-step and 4-step generation, denoted as T1 and T4, respectively, and further evaluate our method on multi-step models, including SDXL with 30 steps and SD v1.4 with 50 steps. Datasets. For feature analysis and fine-tuning data construction, we use a synthetic prompt dataset generated with ChatGPT, containing 50 prompts per concept. For benchmarking concept unlearning, we adopt EvalIGMU benchmark [ 34 ] , which covers four representative concepts: Nudity , VanGogh , Church and Parachute . For robustness evaluation, we further consider three safety-related benchmarks: Inappropriate Image Prompts (I2P) [ 47 ] , Model Manipulation Attack (MMA) dataset [ 48 ] , and the UnlearnDiffAtk method [ 49 ] . Detailed dataset statistics and generation configurations are provided in Appendix B-A . Baselines. We compare our approach against representative unlearning methods, including ESD [ 9 ] , UCE [ 42 ] , ConceptPrune [ 27 ] and SAEUron [ 22 ] . These methods respectively represent fine-tuning-based, model editing, neuron pruning and SAE-based inference approaches. For a fair comparison, we reproduce all baselines on the SDXL-Turbo model following their official implementations. Brief descriptions and implementation details are provided in Appendix B-B . Metrics. We evaluate unlearning performance from four aspects. Unlearning effectiveness is measured using Forgetting Success Rate (FSR), computed by EvalIGMU concept classifiers [ 34 ] , and CLIP Accuracy (CLIP Acc.), which assesses alignment with positive and negative concept anchors in CLIP embedding space [ 50 , 51 , 38 ] . Image quality is evaluated using Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 52 ] . Robustness is assessed by Attack Success Rate (ASR) under adversarial prompting. Finally, we measure unlearning precision using two internal metrics: FO Score and FAC Score proposed in § V , which provide a post-hoc diagnostic of changes in the model’s internal representations during unlearning. sections.heading: VI-B Unlearning Effectiveness
sections.text: Table II reports the FSR and CLIP Acc. across four representative unlearning tasks, and Figure 6 illustrates generated images. Additional visual comparisons with the baselines can be found in Figure 14 in Appendix C-A . As shown in Table II , ConceptACP achieves the highest average FSR and the lowest average CLIP Acc. under both T1 and T4, demonstrating strong unlearning effectiveness. At T1, it improves FSR by 36.34 and reduces CLIP Acc. by 32.10 compared to the best baseline. At T4, it maintains its advantage, improving FSR by 24.10 and reducing CLIP Acc. by 12.48. These results demonstrate that ConceptACP effectively erases target concepts while preserving unrelated content, even under fast-sampling conditions. Observations. We summarize four key observations from our experimental results: First, ESD underperforms mainly due to its dependence on interventions across denoising timesteps. While it typically fine-tunes 50-100 denoising steps on models such as SD v1.4, the 1–4 sampling steps in SDXL-Turbo limit its ability to suppress target concepts, resulting in suboptimal forgetting. In contrast, although trained with single-step generation, ConceptACP generalizes well to multi-step inference, achieving the highest average FSR under T4. Moreover, as shown in Figure 10 in Appendix C-A , the forgetting effect persists across extended generation schedules of up to 30 steps, demonstrating effectiveness across different generation lengths. This is consistent with prior findings [ 41 ] that early timesteps establish coarse layouts and scene composition, making interventions at this stage effective for controlling generation. Second, forgetting for Parachute is less consistent. As illustrated in Figure 6 , ConceptACP removes most instances in many cases, although residual fragments may remain; a detailed analysis is provided in § VII . Other methods often retain substantial portions of the parachute, indicating weaker erasure. Notably, ESD achieves an unusually high FSR of 82.80 under T4, but manual inspection reveals dense, abstract, and cartoonish outputs that are less realistic and semantically coherent than those of ConceptACP . This suggests that a high FSR does not necessarily correspond to better visual quality or more faithful concept removal. Third, for VanGogh in the one-step generation case, we observe that the main subject of the generated images can be affected in Figure 14 in Appendix C-A . This phenomenon can be attributed to two factors: (i) the visualized examples are selected under a trade-off between FSR and FID, and the VanGogh classifier does not always perfectly align with human perception; and (ii) VanGogh represents a global style that inherently influences the entire image. Therefore, for global style concepts such as VanGogh , we do not recommend using an excessively large suppression coefficient a a in practice. We provide a more detailed analysis of this issue in § VI-G . For other concepts and under T4, ConceptACP consistently achieves strong forgetting with comparable image quality and no noticeable degradation. Finally, compared with SAEUron which employs SAEs as external modules, our method achieves notably higher FSRs for Nudity , VanGogh , Church and Parachute , demonstrating the effectiveness of our feature-level fine-tuning strategy. sections.heading: VI-C Unrelated Concept Preservation
sections.text: To assess the impact on unrelated content, we compare FID across tasks in Table II . Overall, ConceptACP maintains competitive FID while achieving stronger forgetting. ESD attains the lowest average FID in T1, consistent with its limited parameter changes and lower FSR. Compared to neuron-level pruning in ConceptPrune, our method delivers substantially higher FSR while keeping comparable FID in T1 (higher by only 2.50 on average) and lower FID in T4 (lower by 6.89 on average). Compared with SAEUron, ConceptACP likewise achieves higher average FSR with only a slight FID increase (1.99 in T1 and 2.73 in T4), demonstrating a favorable trade-off between forgetting and generation quality. UCE achieves the lowest average FID among baselines in T4 but has markedly lower FSR, further highlighting this trade-off.

sections.heading: VI-G Ablation Study
sections.text: Effect of the Regularization Parameter λ \lambda . We analyze the effect of the merge weight λ \lambda on the trade-off between forgetting performance and image quality, with the suppression factor fixed at a = − 5 a=-5 . As illustrated in Figure 9 , smaller λ \lambda values tend to cause under-forgetting, while excessively large values may lead to over-editing and degraded fidelity. Moderate values generally provide the best trade-off. Specifically, λ = 0.2 \lambda=0.2 performs best for Nudity and VanGogh , while λ = 1.8 \lambda=1.8 and λ = 2.0 \lambda=2.0 are optimal for Church and Parachute , respectively. Visual differences across λ \lambda settings are subtle (Figure 11 ), indicating that quantitative metrics are more effective for capturing their effects on concept erasure. Effect of the Scaling Factor a a . We examine how the suppression factor a a affects forgetting performance. As shown in Figure 9 , increasing the magnitude of a a generally improves FSR but may increase FID. Moderate suppression provides the best balance, while excessively strong suppression can over-edit images and reduce visual quality, as illustrated by the VanGogh examples in Figure 12 . Accordingly, we set a = − 8 a=-8 , − 7 -7 , − 9 -9 and − 5 -5 for Nudity , VanGogh , Church and Parachute , respectively. sections.heading: VII Discussion
sections.text: SAE Generality and Concept-Specific Features. Our experiments directly use publicly available general-purpose SAEs, which already provide sufficiently informative features for effective concept localization and unlearning. As shown in Table X in Appendix D , Church and Parachute involve more numerous and dispersed features than Nudity and VanGogh , with Parachute showing relatively weaker forgetting, suggesting that its representation is less cleanly decomposed into sparse features. This suggests an opportunity for further improving feature localization through concept-specific SAE training [ 24 ] , which may yield more concentrated concept-relevant features. Concept Entanglement in Nudity Unlearning. We observe that on the EvalIGMU benchmark, ConceptACP sometimes removes the entire human subject when suppressing Nudity . This is partly influenced by the suppression strength, but more fundamentally, unlike methods [ 9 , 42 ] that steer the target toward a predefined alternative direction (e.g., Clothed ), ConceptACP directly locates and suppresses the features associated with the target concept without specifying a replacement representation, which may lead the model to avoid generating human subjects in some cases to prevent nudity. Importantly, this does not indicate systematic over-forgetting: human subjects remain intact for other prompts, and unrelated-concept evaluations show that human figures can still be generated normally. The observed removal is therefore input-dependent and can be alleviated with milder suppression, as discussed in § VI-G and as shown in Figure 12 in Appendix C-D . Moreover, as noted by SafeGen [ 44 ] , nudity and sexually explicit content are not necessarily equivalent; our unlearning target is specifically nudity rather than sexually explicit content as a whole. This is visually evident in the fourth row of Figure 7 , where generated images still contain sexually suggestive elements, demonstrating the fine-grained and targeted nature of our unlearning.

sections.heading: VIII Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: Conclusion. In this work, we present ConceptACP , a novel unlearning method that transforms interpretability-guided feature interventions into supervision signals for fine-tuning and internalizes their effects into model parameters. By localizing the update to a single cross-attention block, ConceptACP enables efficient and precise concept forgetting without repeatedly running diffusion trajectories or introducing inference-time overhead. Experiments show that ConceptACP achieves superior forgetting performance over SOTA baselines while maintaining image quality, and substantially improves fine-tuning efficiency. Overall, this work bridges interpretability and fine-tuning-based MU, advancing safer and more controllable generative models. Future Work. Future work could explore targeted SAE training approaches that make features related to the target concept more concentrated, as well as feature-selection strategies that adapt across layers and concept types, and strengthen the robustness against stronger adversarial attacks.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: This paper studies concept erasure for text-to-image diffusion models to reduce the generation of undesired content (e.g., NSFW concepts, copyrighted styles, or specific objects) while limiting collateral effects on unrelated content. As with other model-editing techniques, the proposed approach is dual-use: feature localization and targeted modification could be misapplied to disable safety mechanisms or to suppress benign or protected attributes. We therefore frame ConceptACP as a compliance- and safety-oriented unlearning technique and encourage practitioners to apply appropriate governance measures when deploying edited models. Our experiments may involve sensitive prompts and generated outputs; we minimize manual inspection, rely primarily on automated filtering and quantitative evaluation, and avoid displaying explicit content in qualitative examples. This work does not involve new data collection from human subjects or user studies; we use established benchmarks and follow their intended research use and licensing constraints.

sections.heading: Appendix Overview
sections.text: This appendix provides supplementary details and experimental results that complement the main paper. Specifically, the appendix includes: • Appendix A : Feature Localization Algorithm. A formal description of the feature localization procedure used to identify the block and concept-relevant features for targeted unlearning. • Appendix B : Evaluation Details. Detailed descriptions of the evaluation datasets, baseline methods, and metrics used to assess unlearning effectiveness, image quality, robustness, and unlearning precision. • Appendix C : More Evaluation Results. Additional experimental results covering forgetting effectiveness, cross-backbone generalization, robustness against adversarial prompts, multi-concept unlearning, ablation studies, and computational efficiency. • Appendix D : Relevant Features. The concept-relevant SAE features identified by ConceptACP across different concepts and diffusion backbones, together with an analysis of their consistency and diversity.

sections.heading: Appendix A Feature Localization Algorithm
B-A Datasets
sections.text: For computing feature scores and constructing fine-tuning datasets, we use a synthetic dataset generated with ChatGPT, where each concept class contains 50 prompts. For comparison with prior unlearning methods on SDXL-Turbo, we adopt the EvalIGMU benchmark [ 34 ] , which provides 250 prompts for Nudity and VanGogh , and 300 prompts for Church and Parachute . Five images are generated per prompt, resulting in 1,250 images for Nudity and VanGogh , and 1,500 images for Church and Parachute . For experiments on SDXL and SD v1.4, multi-concept unlearning and ablation studies, we generate one image per prompt to reduce computational overhead while maintaining consistent evaluation across settings. For robustness, we use two datasets and one attack method to evaluate our model: • I2P. Inappropriate Image Prompts (I2P) [ 47 ] contains manually curated NSFW text prompts. We select 931 prompts related to sexual content to evaluate robustness in nudity unlearning. • MMA. Model Manipulation Attack dataset (MMA) [ 48 ] contains 1,000 adversarial nudity-targeted prompts and is designed to evaluate robustness in nudity unlearning and the resilience of safety mechanisms under adversarial prompting conditions. • UnlearnDiffAtk. UnlearnDiffAtk [ 49 ] is a white-box attack that perturbs text prompts to bypass unlearning and induce generation of the undesired concept. Since UnlearnDiffAtk was originally developed for SD v1.5, we use the adversarial prompts generated from SD v1.5 to mount a transfer-based attack against SDXL-Turbo backbones to assess the robustness of ConceptACP and the baselines under adversarial prompt manipulations.

sections.heading: B-B Evaluation Baselines
sections.text: We compare our approach against representative unlearning methods spanning fine-tuning, model editing, and inference-time forgetting, and re-implement these methods on SDXL-Turbo for evaluation. The descriptions and implementation details are as follows. • ESD [ 9 ] . A fine-tuning-based unlearning method that use the frozen original model to produce predictions, which are then linearly combined to form a negative guidance signal for updating the new model parameters. For style concepts, ESD fine-tunes the cross-attention parameters, whereas for nudity and object concepts, it fine-tunes the unconditional parameters. We reproduce ESD on SDXL-Turbo under both one-step and four-step fine-tuning settings, and evaluate it correspondingly in one-step and four-step generation. • UCE [ 42 ] . A model-editing based unlearning method that requires no additional training. It modifies the parameters of cross-attention via a closed-form update. The work evaluates concept erasure on attributes such as artistic styles, nudity and gender bias. We reproduce UCE on SDXL-Turbo for evaluation. • ConceptPrune [ 27 ] . A neuron pruning unlearning method that alters model parameters by removing relevant neurons based on an importance score computed for each weight during generating of a specific concept. This work evaluates concept erasure on attributes such as artistic styles, nudity and gender bias. We reproduce ConceptPrune on SDXL-Turbo with four-step generation and use it for both one-step and four-step evaluations. • SAEUron [ 22 ] . An inference-time unlearning method that mounts SAEs on the cross-attention blocks of the SD v1.4 U - Net to suppress target concepts. It focuses on forgetting objects and artistic styles rather than safety-related concepts. We reproduce SAEUron on SDXL-Turbo for evaluation. sections.heading: B-C Metrics
sections.text: We adopt four evaluation metrics to assess the performance of unlearning methods: • [Unlearning Effectiveness] FSR. The Forgetting Success Rate (FSR) is the proportion of generated images that no longer contain the target concept, as determined by a concept detector. The content detectors used here are IGMU_bi_multiC [ 34 ] for Nudity and Style, and IGMU_multi_multiC [ 34 ] for Object. A higher FSR indicates stronger unlearning effectiveness. • [Unlearning Effectiveness] CLIP Acc. Following prior work [ 50 , 51 , 38 ] , we also use CLIP Accuracy (CLIP Acc.) to quantify unlearning effectiveness. For each concept we define two text anchors: a positive anchor A A that describes the concept and a negative anchor B B that is unrelated. Given a generated image I I , let s A = CLIP ⁡ ( I , A ) , s B = CLIP ⁡ ( I , B ) . s_{A}=\mathrm{CLIP}(I,A),\qquad s_{B}=\mathrm{CLIP}(I,B). We classify I I as containing the concept if s A > s B s_{A}>s_{B} ; otherwise it is classified as not containing the concept. CLIP Accuracy is the fraction of images correctly classified under this rule. In our experiments, the positive anchors are “naked”, “van gogh style”, “church” and “parachute” for the four tasks respectively, and the negative anchor is the empty string “ N ​ U ​ L ​ L NULL ”. • [Image Quality] FID Score. Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [ 52 ] measures the distributional distance between generated and reference images. Lower FID indicates better image quality and fidelity after unlearning. Specifically, the generated images are obtained from the fine-tuned model on 𝒟 ¬ c \mathcal{D}_{\neg c} , while the reference images are from the original model on 𝒟 ¬ c \mathcal{D}_{\neg c} . • [Robustness] ASR. The Attack Success Rate (ASR) is the proportion of adversarial prompts that successfully reactivate the forgotten concept. Lower ASR implies stronger robustness against adversarial reactivation. To further evaluate unlearning precision beyond output-level metrics, we report two complementary internal metrics introduced in Section V : • [Unlearning Precision] FO Score. Measures the overlap between the top- K K activated SAE features before and after unlearning for both the target concept and unrelated concepts, capturing whether target-related features are effectively removed while non-target features are preserved. • [Unlearning Precision] FAC Score. Measures the cosine similarity between SAE feature activation distributions before and after unlearning on target and non-target datasets, reflecting distribution-level changes in internal representations.

sections.heading: C-A Forgetting Effectiveness
sections.text: In Figure 14 , we visualize the forgetting results for four concept-specific tasks under different unlearning methods, reporting both single-step and four-step generation for each task. For each concept, we randomly select four images to illustrate the outcomes. These results provide a more direct visual demonstration of the effectiveness of our method. As shown, ConceptACP achieves strong forgetting across all four concepts. In the parachute task, the model successfully removes the parachute-shaped object, although some parachute fabric remnants remain. In Figure 10 , we evaluate the one-step fine-tuned model under up to 30-step image generation. The results show that even for multi-step inference, performing fine-tuning on only a small number of early timesteps is sufficient to achieve effective forgetting of the target concept. This observation is consistent with the findings of Tinaz et al. [ 41 ] , which suggest that early timesteps primarily establish coarse object layouts and scene composition, and interventions at this stage can effectively control the generation process. Effectiveness Across Diffusion Backbones. Beyond the default SDXL-Turbo setting, we further evaluate the effectiveness of ConceptACP under different diffusion backbones and generation step settings. For SDXL, we perform 30-step image generation and collect intermediate representations every five diffusion steps during the denoising process for fine-tuning. The hyperparameters are set to λ = 0.5 \lambda=0.5 and a = − 6 a=-6 for nudity, λ = 0.2 \lambda=0.2 and a = − 6 a=-6 for Van Gogh, λ = 1.8 \lambda=1.8 and a = − 9 a=-9 for church, and λ = 2.0 \lambda=2.0 and a = − 5 a=-5 for parachute. The results on SDXL are reported in Table III . For SD v1.4, the SAEs are adopted from SAEUron [ 22 ] . During fine-tuning, training data are collected every ten diffusion steps, resulting in five sets in total. Both conditional and unconditional SAE reconstructions are included in the fine-tuning process. We use concept-specific hyperparameters, with ( λ , a ) = ( 30 , − 17.5 ) (\lambda,a)=(30,-17.5) for Nudity, ( 8 , − 15 ) (8,-15) for VanGogh, ( 8 , − 20 ) (8,-20) for Church, and ( 15 , − 120 ) (15,-120) for Parachute. The unlearning performance is evaluated under 50-step generation, and the results are reported in Table III . Across both diffusion backbones, ConceptACP achieves effective concept forgetting across diverse target concepts, demonstrating generalization beyond SDXL-Turbo. These results suggest that our representation-guided editing strategy is robust to different diffusion architectures and sampling configurations without requiring architecture-specific modifications.

sections.heading: C-B Robustness
sections.text: In Table VI , we report the attack success rates (ASR) of different unlearning methods against adversarial prompts generated by UnlearnDiffAtk. Although ConceptPrune achieves the lowest average ASR, our method ranks second overall with one best and one second-best result across the four concept tasks. Together with the results on I2P and MMA, these findings indicate that ConceptACP maintains strong overall robustness under both intrinsic and adversarial evaluations. Compared with Table II , we observe that UCE, whose unlearning performance is relatively weak under benign conditions, achieves one best and two second-best ASRs under UnlearnDiffAtk, whereas SAEUron, which previously demonstrates strong forgetting, performs worse in this setting. The inconsistent performance of UCE and SAEUron across evaluations underscores the limited cross-model transferability of such attacks. Developing SDXL-Turbo-specific adversarial forgetting benchmarks would provide a more comprehensive assessment of unlearning robustness.

sections.heading: C-C Multi-concept Unlearning
sections.text: In multi-concept unlearning, we present qualitative results in Figure 13 , which visualize the effects of sequentially erasing Church and Parachute .

Small magnitudes, such as, a = − 3 a=-3 , yield weaker removal of the target concept; for instance, Van Gogh style retains characteristic stars patterns. Increasing | a | \left|a\right| strengthens suppression, and for nudity the person may disappear. However, larger magnitudes can degrade overall image quality. In our experiments, we observe that suppression factors approaching − 10 -10 noticeably reduce aesthetic quality, which we hypothesize arises from imbalance due to overly strong feature activation or suppression. We therefore do not recommend using a < − 10 a<-10 . Efficiency and Resource Overhead. For the efficiency and resource overhead, we evaluate our fine-tuning pipeline on a single NVIDIA A800 GPU (80GB PCIe) with CUDA 12.5 and NVIDIA driver version 555.42.06. Constructing the fine-tuning dataset for 50 prompts takes only 14.07 seconds, which shows that preparing the dataset is highly efficient and does not introduce noticeable overhead. Using precomputed latent input-output pairs, fine-tuning 50 samples for 100 epochs takes 670.3 seconds (11.17 minutes), averaging 6.7 seconds per epoch, excluding data loading and I/O overhead. For comparison, using prompt-based input requires 1,249.7 seconds (20.83 minutes) for the same dataset and epochs, averaging 12.5 seconds per epoch. Latent I/O fine-tuning bypasses the inference stage of the diffusion model and therefore avoids storing intermediate activations, resulting in significantly lower GPU memory consumption and enabling a larger batch size under the same hardware budget. We further observe that enabling automatic mixed-precision (AMP) training reduces the average per-epoch fine-tuning time from 6.7 seconds to 1.34 seconds on SDXL-Turbo and 0.63 seconds on SD v1.4, demonstrating additional efficiency gains. Although the latent-based dataset consumes more storage (71–72 MB) than the prompt-based dataset (28–29 MB), the reduction in fine-tuning time demonstrates a significant efficiency gain. Notably, SAEUron, which performs unlearning via an external SAE module, incurs a 73.3% increase in inference overhead on SDXL-Turbo. In contrast, although our fine-tuning-based approach requires slightly more time upfront to adapt the model, it introduces no additional inference cost. Overall, while maintaining strong forgetting performance, the time overhead of our method remains practical, requiring less than three minutes to forget a single concept. However, existing MU approaches often struggle with the distributed and entangled nature of concept representations, leading to inefficient optimization and imprecise edits when applied through large-scale fine-tuning over full diffusion trajectories. To bridge this gap, we propose Concept Acupuncturist ( ConceptACP ), a novel MU framework that integrates interpretability-guided analysis with inference-free fine-tuning for efficient and precise concept removal. By establishing mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks in the U-Net denoiser and localizing the most concept-relevant block for targeted optimization, ConceptACP avoids full diffusion trajectory optimization, thereby improving fine-tuning efficiency. To mitigate concept entanglement, we propose a feature-level correction mechanism based on Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), where SAE-derived sparse, semantically meaningful feature activations are manipulated to construct targeted correction signals, which are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding block and used as supervision for precise concept removal. Consequently, ConceptACP eliminates the need for external inference-time modules while achieving efficient and fine-grained unlearning. Instantiated on SDXL-Turbo, ConceptACP improves the forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points in the standard one-step generation setting on average over the best-performing baseline, while preserving image quality and prompt fidelity, and generalizes effectively across other Stable Diffusion backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/Eran-Xia/ConceptACP . Warning : This paper includes images that may contain non-explicit nudity and may be sensitive to some readers. I Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] have demonstrated strong capabilities in image synthesis [ 6 , 2 ] and editing [ 7 , 8 ] . Training these models on large-scale web datasets improves performance, but also exposes them to diverse and weakly curated content. Consequently, such models may produce harmful or policy-violating content, e.g., Not-Safe-For-Work (NSFW) imagery [ 9 , 10 ] or infringing outputs that replicate protected identities or artistic styles without authorization [ 11 ] . These concerns motivate the development of various strategies for mitigating unsafe content, including dataset curation, post-processing and direct model modification. However, retraining on filtered datasets is often computationally expensive [ 12 , 13 ] , and post-processing remains vulnerable to prompt manipulation [ 14 , 15 ] . Approaches for direct model modification, particularly machine unlearning (MU), offer a more direct and controllable way to remove specific concepts without full retraining [ 16 , 17 ] . Existing MU methods can be broadly divided into three categories: inference-time intervention, model editing and fine-tuning-based unlearning. Inference-time approaches [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] typically suppress undesirable concepts by attaching external, removable modules during inference, which modify model outputs without altering model parameters and thus leave concept-related representations encoded within the model. Such interventions may introduce artifacts and degrade generation quality [ 25 ] , while their inference overhead becomes non-negligible under large-scale deployment. Model editing methods [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] directly modify model parameters through closed-form or localized updates to remove target concepts. However, the highly distributed and entangled representations in diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 ] make precise parameter localization difficult. More fundamentally, existing methods focus on finding low-interference update directions rather than identifying the parameters or internal features that encode the target concept [ 28 ] . Fine-tuning-based MU methods, in contrast, directly modify model parameters without additional inference overhead, making them widely adopted for safer image generation. However, they still face two fundamental challenges: (i) limited edit precision, since global or layer-wise updates often interfere with unrelated concepts due to the polysemantic nature of neurons [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , making it difficult to precisely remove a target concept without affecting others; and (ii) high computational cost, as they often update a large portion of model parameters (e.g., all cross-attention layers or global weights [ 9 , 32 ] ) and require executing the denoising process up to an intermediate timestep to obtain supervision [ 9 ] due to the iterative nature of diffusion models, thereby incurring full-trajectory cost even for local updates and leading to substantial training overhead, especially when scaling to multiple concepts or iterative updates. To overcome these limitations, we propose Concept Acupuncturist ( ConceptACP ), a structured fine-tuning framework that enables inference-free and localized updates for parameter optimization. Inspired by recent interpretability studies showing that concept-related information can be decomposed into structured and semantically meaningful components [ 33 ] , we introduce Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), an interpretable tool that decomposes neuron activations into sparse feature representations within the U-Net denoiser, to enable fine-grained concept removal. We further reformulate diffusion fine-tuning as a localized block-level learning problem, avoiding full denoising trajectories during optimization. Nevertheless, realizing this design presents two technical challenges: C1: difficulty in internalizing feature-level interventions into model parameters. Existing SAE-based methods typically treat SAEs as inference-time intervention modules [ 22 , 23 ] . A natural question is therefore whether the benefits of such feature-level editing can be directly embedded into model parameters. However, SAEs operate on the residual updates of corresponding blocks and require explicit feature manipulation to achieve forgetting, making their direct translation into parameter updates non-trivial. C2: difficulty in identifying the target block and constructing reliable supervision signals. Concept representations in diffusion models are distributed across multiple cross-attention blocks and evolve over the denoising trajectory, making it challenging to identify an appropriate block and derive consistent supervision for localized fine-tuning. To address C1 , we move beyond treating SAEs as external modules but as a mechanism for constructing supervision signals. Given prompts containing the target concept, we identify concept-relevant features and suppress them according to their relevance scores via a feature selection procedure. The modified features are then projected back to the output space of the corresponding cross-attention block. This process yields target outputs that are equivalent to performing feature-level editing, but expressed in the model’s native representation space. By pairing these corrected outputs with the original inputs, we construct a supervision dataset that enables internalization of feature-level interventions into model parameters. To address C2 , we reformulate diffusion fine-tuning as a localized block-level learning problem. Specifically, we establish mappings between semantic concepts and cross-attention blocks using a pool of pretrained SAEs, building upon prior analysis [ 33 ] . Based on the mappings, we identify one block most strongly associated with the target concept together with its relevant features and then construct a block-level input–output supervision dataset from a small set of text prompts at selected timesteps. The target outputs are obtained via the feature-level correction process described above. Importantly, we collect the block’s activations across timesteps in a single forward pass, avoiding repeated denoising during fine-tuning while retaining further flexible feature manipulation through the cached activations. We implement ConceptACP on SDXL-Turbo and evaluate it on the EvalIGMU [ 34 ] benchmark across four representative concepts. Experiments show that ConceptACP achieves strong balance between forgetting effectiveness and preservation of unrelated concepts, improving forgetting success rate by 36.34 percentage points on average under the standard one-step setting over the best-performing baseline. We further observe consistent gains on SDXL and SD v1.4, demonstrating transferability across backbones. In terms of efficiency, our block-level, inference-free fine-tuning reduces computational cost by 46.4% compared to full diffusion-based method without this design. In addition, we introduce two metrics, Feature Overlap Score and Feature Activation Correlation Score , to characterize internal feature dynamics before and after unlearning. Results show that our method induces feature-level changes consistent with the intended concept suppression and non-target preservation, providing internal evidence for its precise unlearning. Additional results demonstrate preserved image quality and robustness against adversarial prompts. Our main contributions are outlined below: • We propose ConceptACP , a novel unlearning framework that integrates interpretability-guided feature analysis into parameter-level fine-tuning for diffusion models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to use SAE-derived feature corrections as supervision for localized and internalized fine-tuning in diffusion model unlearning. • We introduce a structured fine-tuning paradigm that jointly improves edit precision and efficiency. For precision, we use SAE-derived feature corrections as fine-grained supervision, while for efficiency, we construct block-level input–output supervision to enable inference-free fine-tuning of a single cross-attention block. • Extensive experiments show that ConceptACP effectively removes target concepts while preserving model utility and substantially reducing fine-tuning computational cost. II Background and Related Work II-A Text-to-Image Models Diffusion models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] synthesize realistic images by gradually denoising random noise through a learned reverse diffusion process. These models typically consist of three key components: a text encoder that converts input prompts into semantic embeddings, a U - Net denoiser that conditions on the text embedding and iteratively refines a latent representation, and a decoder that maps the latent representation back to the image space. Among these components, the U - Net serves as the core of the denoising process, comprising downsampling and upsampling pathways connected through residual blocks, often interleaved with attention or transformer modules. Traditional Stable Diffusion models, such as the 1.x and 2.x versions, typically require tens of denoising steps (e.g., 50) to generate high-quality images. To improve image fidelity and prompt adherence, Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) [ 5 ] was introduced. SDXL-Turbo [ 35 ] , on the other hand, is a distilled variant of SDXL, trained with techniques such as adversarial and progressive distillation to accelerate generation. It typically requires only 1–4 steps to generate an image while maintaining competitive visual quality. Architecturally, the U - Net in SDXL-Turbo comprises a downsampling path, a bottleneck section and an upsampling path with transformer blocks to capture global context. With growing demand for real-time and interactive text-to-image generation, SDXL-Turbo has gained significant attention for its fast inference. II-B Machine Unlearning MU aims to remove the influence of specific subsets of data or learned knowledge from a trained model [ 36 , 37 ] . Typically, existing methods for T2I models either erase individual samples or suppress undesired concepts. The latter, which has received substantial attention in recent studies, aims to significantly suppress the T2I model’s ability to generate particular undesired concepts while preserving its performance on unrelated content. The unlearning targets explored in prior research include: (1) semantics (e.g., nudity, violence, and gore), (2) stylistic attributes (e.g., Van Gogh), and (3) objects (e.g., church and parachute). Existing MU approaches can be broadly categorized into three strategies: Model Fine-tuning. Fine-tuning-based methods achieve unlearning by updating model parameters to erase target concepts. For example, ESD [ 9 ] shifts predictions from concept-conditioned to unconditional outputs, AC [ 38 ] align distributions for concept removal, SA [ 39 ] replaces forgotten concepts with alternative distributions, attention redirection [ 11 ] fine-tunes cross-attention layers, MACE [ 40 ] combines attention editing with LoRA for multi-concept erasure, and TRACE [ 32 ] constrains edits to later denoising stages. Model Editing. Model editing-based approaches aim to remove concepts without additional training by directly modifying model weights. RECE [ 26 ] iteratively eliminates residual embeddings, and ConceptPrune [ 27 ] prunes FFN neurons correlated with the target concept. SPEED [ 28 ] further improves prior preservation by introducing null-space constrained parameter editing, where model updates are restricted to directions that minimize interference with non-target concepts. Inference-time Intervention. Inference intervention-based methods manipulate prompts or feature activations during inference. SLD [ 18 ] appends concept descriptors to prompts, SAFREE [ 19 ] projects toxic token embeddings orthogonally to harmful concepts, TraSCE [ 20 ] provides trajectory-level guidance, and SafeRedir [ 21 ] redirects the prompt embeddings of unsafe concepts. Based on Sparse Autoencoders, SAEUron [ 22 ] trains them on U - Net feature activations, ConceptSteerers [ 23 ] applies SAEs to the text encoder, and SAEmnesia [ 24 ] uses supervised SAE training for clearer concept-neuron mapping. II-D Threat Model With the rapid progress of generative artificial intelligence, diffusion-based image generation models have been widely deployed in online platforms and local applications. However, this flexibility also raises safety and copyright concerns, as users may intentionally generate inappropriate content (e.g., nudity, violence) or unintentionally produce images that mimic copyrighted artistic styles (e.g., Van Gogh). We consider two realistic deployment scenarios for T2I diffusion models in practical deployment settings. S1: Online Deployment with Controlled Access. In this setting, the service provider deploys the diffusion model online and exposes its interface for user interaction under controlled conditions. The adversaries seek to induce the model to generate unsafe or policy-violating images. Their access to the model is strictly black-box: they can only interact with the system through text prompts and observe the generated outputs. As a result, adversaries may attempt prompt-based attacks, such as carefully crafted or obfuscated prompts, to bypass safety filters in online deployments. S2: Public Release of Model Checkpoints. We assume that the model providers who host or distribute text-to-image diffusion models are trusted. Their goal is to maintain a balance between safety and utility, preventing the generation of harmful or undesired content while preserving the model’s ability to produce benign and creative outputs. In practice, such providers may share model checkpoints with the research community. Adversaries can download the released model weights and deploy the model locally with full control. They can attempt low-cost strategies to bypass safety mechanisms, e.g., by removing external modules or directly querying the base model without the added controls. Under this setting, the model provider does not bear responsibility for any consequences resulting from downstream modification to the model weights. III Empirical Study MU methods in diffusion models have evolved rapidly in recent years. However, many design choices, including localization strategy, editing paradigm, optimization scope and evaluation protocol, remain largely empirical. In this section, we systematically investigate these design choices through a series of empirical studies. Our findings not only reveal the limitations of existing approaches but also motivate the design principles adopted in ConceptACP . III-A The Limitations of Neuron-level Localization Unlearning methods must first determine where to edit, as precise localization enables effective concept removal with minimal interference to unrelated concepts. Existing approaches perform localization at different levels of the network. For example, ESD [ 9 ] modifies model parameters globally, UCE [ 42 ] edits concept representations through cross-attention layers, and ConceptPrune [ 27 ] identifies and suppresses concept-related neurons in the FFN modules of the U-Net. However, these approaches still rely on neuron-level or architecture-level localization, which faces fundamental challenges due to the polysemantic nature of neurons [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , where a single neuron may encode information about multiple concepts, hindering selective concept removal. As shown in Table III , although existing methods achieve considerable forgetting success rates, they often degrade image quality, suggesting that coarse localization can affect representations beyond the target concept. While recent methods such as SPEED [ 28 ] improve the preservation of unrelated concepts by constraining parameter updates to less interfering subspaces, they mainly focus on how to edit after selecting the editing space. However, achieving precise unlearning also requires addressing where to edit , i.e., accurately identifying the internal representations associated with the target concept. SAEs provide a potential solution by decomposing polysemantic neurons into more sparse and interpretable features, motivating feature-level localization for more precise concept unlearning. In Figure 1 , we visualize the six most highly activated SAE features across four representative cross-attention blocks for the same input. Notably, visual features associated with the naked concept show strong activation in the down.2.1 cross-attention block. This observation indicates that concepts are localized to specific internal representations rather than uniformly distributed across the network. Observation 1: Neuron-level localization is insufficient for precise concept removal due to neuron polysemanticity, often affecting unrelated representations and degrading generation quality. III-B The Fragility of Inference-time Steering Instead of modifying model parameters, inference-time unlearning methods perform concept suppression during inference by introducing external modules or modifying the generation pipeline. However, such approaches remain fragile due to their bypassability in open-source settings and the additional computation incurred for each generation. As shown in Table I , we evaluate three representative methods (TraSCE [ 20 ] , SAFREE [ 19 ] and SAEUron [ 22 ] ) on SDXL-Turbo and observe that they introduce 14.4%–125.8% additional inference latency, which translates into continuous computational expenses during deployment despite avoiding one-time editing costs. In contrast, parameter editing incurs a one-time cost with zero inference overhead, whereas inference-time steering incurs continuous overhead that accumulates with the number of requests. Using a representative GPU serving cost of $4/hour based on on-demand NVIDIA A100 pricing and the original SDXL-Turbo latency of 0.6848 seconds (Table IX ), the measured overhead translates to approximately $110–$960 additional cost per million generation requests, which is non-negligible at scale. Moreover, SAEUron leverages SAEs for targeted inference-time suppression but directly manipulates intermediate representations, potentially disturbing the original feature distribution and introducing visual artifacts [ 25 ] . Together with the inference overhead discussed above, these limitations make direct parameter editing a more robust alternative, as it permanently modifies the model without additional inference cost. III-C The Inefficiency of Large-scale Fine-tuning Existing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods [ 9 , 40 , 32 ] suffer from substantial computational overhead due to both large-scale parameter updates and the iterative nature of diffusion models. These methods typically modify a large portion of model parameters (e.g., multiple cross-attention layers or global weights), while obtaining supervision at a specific denoising timestep requires executing all preceding steps. Consequently, updating even a local module remains coupled with the full denoising trajectory, leading to inefficient optimization. As shown in Table VIII , fine-tuning a single cross-attention block without executing the complete denoising trajectory reduces the per-iteration training time to 53.6% of the original approach. This demonstrates that a significant portion of the optimization cost comes from the dependency on the full diffusion trajectory rather than the actual parameters being updated. This highlights the substantial computational overhead of large-scale fine-tuning, which is not necessarily accompanied by improved concept forgetting. Observation 3: Existing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods incur substantial optimization costs due to large-scale parameter updates and full-trajectory dependency, while local updates may achieve comparable forgetting with substantially lower cost. III-D The Limitations of Output-based Evaluation Fig. 2: Discrepancy between classifier-based evaluation and human perception after concept unlearning. Existing diffusion unlearning methods are typically evaluated through generated outputs, where classifiers are used to determine whether the target concept remains present after unlearning. However, classifier-based evaluation may not accurately reflect human perception, resulting in discrepancies between automated assessment and actual visual understanding. As illustrated in Figure 2 , generated images that receive similar classifier predictions may exhibit different levels of concept presence from a human perspective. Therefore, output-level metrics alone provide incomplete evidence of genuine concept forgetting. Analyzing internal representations associated with visual concepts can provide complementary insights into the forgetting process, yet remains largely unexplored so far in existing works. Observation 4: Output-level evaluation provides incomplete evidence of concept forgetting as classifier predictions may not align with human perception, motivating complementary analysis of internal representations. III-E The Generalization Gap Across Diffusion Architectures Most existing MU methods were developed for Stable Diffusion v1.4/1.5. However, modern diffusion models such as SDXL-Turbo introduce substantial differences in model architecture and inference, including deeper U-Net structures and significantly fewer sampling steps. When directly applied to SDXL-Turbo, existing methods exhibit notable performance degradation (e.g., ESD), which we hypothesize is partly due to its fast-sampling regime (1–4 vs. tens of steps in standard SD). Quantitative results and visualizations (see § VI-B ) further support these limitations under fast-sampling conditions. Observation 5: Existing unlearning methods, particularly timestep-wise interventions, show limited cross-architecture generalization, as SD1.x-based approaches degrade significantly on modern fast-sampling models. Overall, these observations highlight the need for unlearning approaches that are both precise and effective across different diffusion paradigms, including traditional multi-step diffusion models as well as modern large-scale, fast-sampling ones, as addressed by the method proposed in this work.
